questions.stem: Ultrasound is used in prenatal scans rather than X-rays. What is the main reason for this choice?

options.text: Ultrasound produces clearer images than X-rays
Ultrasound is non-ionising and does not harm the developing baby, unlike X-rays which are ionising
Ultrasound travels faster than X-rays through the body
X-rays cannot penetrate the human body

questions.explanation: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves, which are non-ionising and safe for both mother and baby. X-rays are ionising electromagnetic radiation that can damage DNA and harm a developing foetus. Option A is incorrect — X-rays can produce very detailed images of bones. Option D is incorrect — X-rays do penetrate the body (that is how they create images).

questions.stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into the body and reflects off a structure. The pulse takes 0.00004 seconds to return. If the speed of ultrasound in body tissue is 1540 m/s, how deep is the structure?
questions.explanation: Total distance = speed x time = 1540 x 0.00004 = 0.0616 m. Since the pulse travels to the structure and back, the depth = 0.0616 / 2 = 0.0308 m (about 3.08 cm). Option A (0.0616 m) is the round-trip distance — a common error in echo/reflection calculations is forgetting to halve the distance.

questions.stem: Ultrasound is defined as sound with a frequency above:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is sound above the upper limit of human hearing, which is approximately 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). The human hearing range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Option A (20 Hz) is the lower limit of human hearing. Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound.

questions.stem: A ship uses sonar to detect the ocean floor. An ultrasound pulse takes 0.1 seconds to return. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. What is the depth of the ocean at that point?
questions.explanation: Total distance = speed x time = 1500 x 0.1 = 150 m. The pulse travels down to the floor and back up, so depth = 150 / 2 = 75 m. Option A (150 m) forgets to halve the distance. Option D (15,000) multiplies incorrectly. Always remember to divide by 2 in echo/sonar calculations.

questions.stem: Ultrasound can be used to detect cracks inside metal railway tracks. How does this work?

options.text: Ultrasound melts the metal around cracks, making them visible
Ultrasound pulses reflect off boundaries between different materials, so a crack creates an unexpected reflection that shows up on the display
Ultrasound passes through cracks more easily than through metal
Cracks absorb ultrasound, creating dark spots in the image

questions.explanation: Ultrasound reflects at boundaries between different materials (metal and air inside the crack). An unexpected reflection returning earlier than the expected back-wall reflection indicates a crack at that depth. The timing of the reflection reveals how deep the crack is. This is a non-destructive testing method, unlike cutting the track open to inspect it.
